Algorithm reference: core COHALU functions

Source: vignettes/algorithms.Rmd
algorithms.Rmd

This vignette documents the mathematics behind each core function in COHALU. The formulas mirror the implementation in R/cohalu_functions.R line-by-line, not a stylized version.

library(cohalu)
#> Loading cohalu v0.99.3: COHALU - CO-localization, Hotspots And sample-Level Units (formerly spatialCooccur).
#> To cite this package in publications, please use:
#>   Inamo J, et al. (2026). Spatial transcriptomics reveals  immune-stromal crosstalk within the synovium of patients with  juvenile idiopathic arthritis. JCI Insight. 11(1):e198074.  doi:10.1172/jci.insight.198074
#> Developed by: Jun Inamo <juninamo@keio.jp>

Notation

Throughout, a sample is a finite set of cells

𝒱={v1,…,vN},𝐱v∈ℝ2,c(v)∈𝒞={c1,…,cK}, \mathcal{V} = \{v_1, \dots, v_N\}, \quad \mathbf{x}_v \in \mathbb{R}^{2}, \quad c(v) \in \mathcal{C} = \{c_1, \dots, c_K\},

where 𝐱v\mathbf{x}_v is the 2-D centroid and c(v)c(v) the discrete cluster label (e.g. cell type). For each function we additionally use:

  • A∈{0,1}N×NA \in \{0, 1\}^{N \times N} — adjacency of a kk-nearest-neighbor (kNN) graph on {𝐱v}\{\mathbf{x}_v\}, with Auv=1A_{uv} = 1 iff vv is one of the kk nearest neighbors of uu (the cell itself included). Built exactly with a kd-tree (RANN::nn2(coords, k = k)).
  • dv=∑uAuvd_v = \sum_u A_{uv} — the (in-)degree of vv in the kNN graph.
  • Nr(v)={u∈𝒱\{v}:‖𝐱u−𝐱v‖≤r}N_r(v) = \{u \in \mathcal{V}\setminus\{v\} : \lVert \mathbf{x}_u - \mathbf{x}_v \rVert \le r\} — radius-rr neighborhood, computed with RANN::nn2(..., searchtype = "radius", radius = r, k = k_\max).
  • 𝒱c={v:c(v)=c}\mathcal{V}_c = \{v : c(v) = c\} — the set of cells in cluster cc.

generate_sim() — synthetic spatial layouts

generate_sim() produces a single sample under one of three generative schemes. The user supplies close_ratio ρ\rho, distance_param Δ\Delta, n_cells NN, n_types KK, and max_loc LL (the side length of the bounding box).

In every case the non-special cells are drawn uniformly from 𝒰([0,L]2)\mathcal{U}\bigl([0, L]^2\bigr) and the cluster labels are sampled i.i.d. from a uniform distribution over {c1,…,cK}\{c_1, \dots, c_K\}. What differs between test_types is how cell_type_1 and cell_type_2 are positioned.

test_type = "distribute"

Start from NN i.i.d. samples in [0,L]2[0, L]^2 with i.i.d. cluster labels. Let Ik={v:c(v)=ck}I_k = \{v : c(v) = c_k\} denote the index set of cluster kk. A fraction ρ\rho of cell_type_2 cells, of size

npair=round(ρ⋅|I2|), n_\text{pair} = \mathrm{round}\bigl(\rho \cdot |I_2|\bigr),

is randomly chosen and moved to be near a uniformly random cell_type_1 cell:

θm∼iid𝒰(0,2π),𝛈m∼iid𝒩(𝟎,(Δ/5)2I2), \theta_m \stackrel{\text{iid}}{\sim} \mathcal{U}(0, 2\pi), \quad \boldsymbol{\eta}_m \stackrel{\text{iid}}{\sim} \mathcal{N}\!\left(\mathbf{0},\, (\Delta/5)^2 I_2\right),

𝐱vm(2)←𝐱vm(1)+Δ(cos⁡θmsin⁡θm)+𝛈m,m=1,…,npair, \mathbf{x}_{v_m^{(2)}} \;\leftarrow\; \mathbf{x}_{v_m^{(1)}} \;+\; \Delta \binom{\cos \theta_m}{\sin \theta_m} \;+\; \boldsymbol{\eta}_m, \quad m = 1, \dots, n_\text{pair},

where (vm(1),vm(2))(v_m^{(1)}, v_m^{(2)}) are randomly paired indices from I1I_1 and I2I_2. So ρ\rho controls how many type-2 cells are seeded next to a type-1 cell, and Δ\Delta controls how close the pair is.

test_type = "circle"

generate_sim() sets the disk centre at 𝐜=(L/2,L/2)\mathbf{c} = (L/2, L/2) and the radius at R=⌈L/6⌉R = \lceil L/6 \rceil. Of n1=⌈N/K⌉n_1 = \lceil N/K \rceilcell_type_1 cells, a fraction ρ\rho is placed inside / on the disk:

n1close=round(ρn1),outer ring:𝐱v=𝐜+R(cos⁡θ,sin⁡θ),θ∈uniform grid on [0,2π],inner disk:𝐱v=𝐜+ρv(cos⁡θv,sin⁡θv),ρv=UvR,Uv∼𝒰(0,1),θv∼𝒰(0,2π), \begin{aligned} n_1^{\text{close}} &= \mathrm{round}(\rho \, n_1), \\ \text{outer ring:} \quad \mathbf{x}_v &= \mathbf{c} + R\,(\cos\theta, \sin\theta), \quad \theta \in \text{uniform grid on } [0, 2\pi], \\ \text{inner disk:} \quad \mathbf{x}_v &= \mathbf{c} + \rho_v (\cos\theta_v, \sin\theta_v), \quad \rho_v = \sqrt{U_v}\,R, \; U_v \sim \mathcal{U}(0, 1), \; \theta_v \sim \mathcal{U}(0, 2\pi), \end{aligned}

with the remaining n1−n1closen_1 - n_1^\text{close} cells dropped uniformly in [0,L]2[0, L]^2. Of n2=⌈N/K⌉n_2 = \lceil N/K \rceilcell_type_2 cells, n2close=round(ρn2)n_2^\text{close} = \mathrm{round}(\rho \, n_2) are placed on the outer ring R+ΔR + \Delta:

𝐱v=𝐜+(R+Δ)(cos⁡θ,sin⁡θ)+𝛈,𝛈∼𝒩(𝟎,52I2). \mathbf{x}_v = \mathbf{c} + (R + \Delta)\,(\cos\theta, \sin\theta) + \boldsymbol{\eta}, \quad \boldsymbol{\eta} \sim \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0}, 5^2 I_2).

The remainder of cell_type_2 is uniform, as are the other K−2K - 2 clusters. The result is the familiar “type-1 disk + type-2 ring” layout: the two clusters co-occur at the scale of the whole disk, but a small-kk local neighborhood graph mostly sees same-cluster neighbors.

test_type = "line"

Two thin horizontal layers separated vertically by Δ\Delta. Layer 0 contains cell_type_1 along an evenly spaced xx-axis grid with Gaussian jitter; layer 1 contains cell_type_2 at yy-position shifted by Δ\Delta. A fraction ρ\rho of layer-1 cells are snapped to the (x,y+Δ)(x, y + \Delta) position of a randomly chosen layer-0 cell, so that ρ\rho again controls how many cell_type_2 cells are tightly paired with a cell_type_1 cell.

nhood_enrichment() — neighbourhood enrichment

Step 1 — build the kNN adjacency

Construct the exact kNN graph with a kd-tree (RANN::nn2(coords, k = k); the cell counts as its own neighbour, as in Seurat::FindNeighbors). Let A∈{0,1}N×NA \in \{0, 1\}^{N \times N} be the resulting adjacency, or, with connectivity_key = "snn", Seurat’s shared-nearest-neighbour matrix.

Step 2 — degree weighting (optional, off by default)

By default (transformation = FALSE) every kNN link counts once, as in squidpy. When transformation = TRUE, each link from cell uu is divided by the number of cells that chose uu as a neighbour (plus one), which mildly down-weights “hub” cells chosen by many others. With a kNN graph every cell sends kk links at any density and dud_u averages kk in both dense and sparse tissue; it differs mainly at density transitions (e.g. cells just outside a dense cluster are chosen less often). Density itself is handled by the label shuffles, which keep every position. In simulations the weighting kept the calibration but lowered power (planted pair, 1,500 cells: 14% vs 28%), so it is off by default:

Ãuv=Auvdu+1,du=∑wAwu. \tilde A_{uv} \;=\; \frac{A_{uv}}{d_u + 1}, \qquad d_u = \sum_{w} A_{wu}.

Otherwise Ã=A\tilde A = A and the function counts edges as binary.

Step 3 — cluster-pair count matrix

For every ordered cluster pair (ci,cj)(c_i, c_j), sum entries of Ã\tilde A whose row cell belongs to cic_i and column cell to cjc_j:

Cij=∑u∈𝒱ci∑v∈𝒱cjÃuv. C_{ij} \;=\; \sum_{u \in \mathcal{V}_{c_i}} \sum_{v \in \mathcal{V}_{c_j}} \tilde A_{uv}.

This is the observed value, implemented in compute_count() as M⊤ÃMM^\top \tilde A M with one-hot cluster indicators MM.

Step 4 — permutation null

permute_clusters() draws one uniform random permutation π(b)\pi^{(b)} of the cluster labels and applies it to rows and columns alike, so every cell keeps a single (random) label, and recomputes the count:

Cij(b)=∑u∈𝒱ci(π(b))∑v∈𝒱cj(π(b))Ãuv,b=1,…,B. C^{(b)}_{ij} \;=\; \sum_{u \in \mathcal{V}^{(\pi^{(b)})}_{c_i}} \sum_{v \in \mathcal{V}^{(\pi^{(b)})}_{c_j}} \tilde A_{uv}, \quad b = 1, \dots, B.

Positions, the graph and the number of cells of each type are fixed; only which type sits where is random. (Versions ≤\le 0.99.1 shuffled rows and columns independently, which inflated same-type z-scores.)

Step 5 — effect size: centred log2 O/E

With Eij=1B∑bCij(b)E_{ij} = \frac{1}{B}\sum_b C^{(b)}_{ij} and a pseudocount cc of one mean edge weight,

ℓij=log⁡2Cij+cEij+c,log2_oeij=ℓij−1B∑blog⁡2Cij(b)+cEij+c \ell_{ij} = \log_2\frac{C_{ij} + c}{E_{ij} + c}, \qquad \boxed{\;\mathrm{log2\_oe}_{ij} \;=\; \ell_{ij} - \frac{1}{B}\sum_{b}\log_2\frac{C^{(b)}_{ij} + c}{E_{ij} + c}\;}

The log of a ratio of small counts is biased below 0 (Jensen), so rare cell types get ℓij<0\ell_{ij} < 0 without any interaction. Subtracting the mean of the same statistic over the shuffles centres it at 0 under the null for any number of cells. ℓij\ell_{ij} is returned as log2_oe_raw. log2_oe does not grow with the number of cells and is the value to compare between samples.

Step 6 — within-sample test: pvalue and padj

For each unordered pair the two directions are summed, Sij=Cij+CjiS_{ij} = C_{ij} + C_{ji} (Sii=CiiS_{ii} = C_{ii}), and standardised together with the shuffles, using the mean μij\mu_{ij} and SD sijs_{ij} of the B+1B + 1 values {Sij,Sij(1),…,Sij(B)}\{S_{ij}, S^{(1)}_{ij}, \dots, S^{(B)}_{ij}\}:

zij=|Sij−μij|sij,pvalueij=2Φ(−zij). z_{ij} = \frac{|S_{ij} - \mu_{ij}|}{s_{ij}}, \qquad \mathrm{pvalue}_{ij} = 2\,\Phi(-z_{ij}).

pvalue is accurate for a single pre-specified pair. For all K(K+1)/2K(K+1)/2 pairs at once, padj is the Westfall–Young single-step max-T adjusted p-value

padjij=1+#{b:maxklzkl(b)≥zij}B+1 \boxed{\;\mathrm{padj}_{ij} \;=\; \frac{1 + \#\{b : \max_{kl} z^{(b)}_{kl} \ge z_{ij}\}}{B + 1}\;}

which controls the family-wise error rate and adapts to the skewed, dependent null of rare pairs (Benjamini–Hochberg on pvalue, returned as padj_bh, can exceed its level when there are many rare cell types). The smallest possible padj is 1/(B+1)1/(B+1). The unsymmetrised zij=(Cij−Eij)/SD(Cij(b))z_{ij} = (C_{ij} - E_{ij}) / \mathrm{SD}(C^{(b)}_{ij}) is still returned as zscore; it grows with the number of cells.

Step 7 — directional statistics: contact and dominance

Every ii–jj contact is also a jj–ii contact, so the pair-level O/E is (nearly) symmetric: O/Ei→j=share of j among the neighbours of ipj≈share of i among the neighbours of jpi\mathrm{O/E}_{i\to j} = \frac{\text{share of } j \text{ among the neighbours of } i}{p_j} \approx \frac{\text{share of } i \text{ among the neighbours of } j}{p_i}. It answers “is there more ii–jj contact than chance?”, not “from whose point of view”. The heatmap of plot_nhood_heatmap(value = "log2_oe") shows the average of the two directions, once per pair (lower triangle). Two directional questions (row = centre cell type ii, column = neighbour type jj) are answered on the unweighted kk-NN graph without the cell itself, with nu,jn_{u,j} the number of type-jj neighbours of cell uu and dud_u its number of neighbours:

contactij=1ni∑u∈i1[nu,j≥1],dominanceij=1ni∑u∈i1[nu,j≥du/2]. \mathrm{contact}_{ij} = \frac{1}{n_i}\sum_{u \in i} 1[n_{u,j} \ge 1], \qquad \mathrm{dominance}_{ij} = \frac{1}{n_i}\sum_{u \in i} 1[n_{u,j} \ge d_u / 2].

contact asks how much of population ii touches jj; dominance asks whether the neighbourhoods of ii are dominated by jj. Both are compared with the same label shuffles (*_expected, centred *_log2_oe), tested per ordered pair (*_pvalue) and adjusted by max-T over all K2K^2 ordered pairs (*_padj). For a rare type AA that always sits inside clusters of an abundant type BB, dominance[A, B] is enriched and dominance[B, A] is not, while contact[B, A] is enriched (more BB cells than expected touch an AA) and contact[A, B] saturates near 1. Read the two together.

In code:

res <- nhood_enrichment(df, cluster_key = "cell_type", neighbors.k = 10,
                        n_perms = 200, seed = 1, n_jobs = 1)
res$log2_oe   # effect size (centred)
res$padj      # max-T adjusted, all pairs
plot_nhood_heatmap(res)                               # pair level (symmetric)
plot_nhood_heatmap(res, value = "dominance_log2_oe")  # directional

calc_co_occurrence_for_radius() and compute_co_occurrence_ratio()

Where nhood_enrichment() works on a fixed-kk graph, these two functions work on a fixed-radius neighborhood and report a conditional-probability ratio instead of a z-score.

Step 1 — radius-based neighbor counts

For each cell vv, find its radius neighborhood Nr(v)N_r(v) via RANN::nn2 (with cap kk). Tally pairs by cluster:

Cij=∑v∈𝒱ci|Nr(v)∩𝒱cj|. C_{ij} \;=\; \sum_{v \in \mathcal{V}_{c_i}}\; \bigl|N_r(v) \cap \mathcal{V}_{c_j}\bigr|.

Note that the same physical pair (v,u)(v, u) contributes once to Cc(v),c(u)C_{c(v), c(u)} and once to Cc(u),c(v)C_{c(u), c(v)}, so CC is symmetric when accumulated over all cells. The matrix is stored under co_occur_count.

Step 2 — enrichment ratio

compute_co_occurrence_ratio() then converts CC to a ratio of empirical probabilities (Lifshitz / Giotto convention):

P(j∣i)=Cij∑kCik,P(j)=∑kCkj∑k,lCkl, P(j \mid i) \;=\; \frac{C_{ij}}{\sum_k C_{ik}}, \qquad P(j) \;=\; \frac{\sum_k C_{kj}}{\sum_{k, l} C_{kl}},

rij=P(j∣i)P(j). \boxed{\; r_{ij} \;=\; \frac{P(j \mid i)}{P(j)}\;. }

rij>1r_{ij} > 1 means a cell in cluster cic_i is more likely to have a cluster-cjc_j neighbor than chance predicts from the overall pair composition. Unlike the z-score in §nhood_enrichment(), this ratio is deterministic — no permutation is run.

cooccur_local() — per-cell local co-occurrence

Where the previous two functions produce a cluster-pair matrix, this one produces a per-cell score for a single pair (cx,cy)(c_x, c_y) chosen by the caller. It is meant to highlight individual cells that sit at the interface of two cluster populations.

Step 1 — local presence indicator

Take the radius-rr neighborhood Nr(v)N_r(v) (with neighbor cap kk). The raw local co-occurrence score is

sv(0)=𝟙{Nr(v)∩𝒱cx≠∅∧Nr(v)∩𝒱cy≠∅}. s_v^{(0)} \;=\; \mathbb{1}\!\left\{ N_r(v) \cap \mathcal{V}_{c_x} \ne \emptyset \;\wedge\; N_r(v) \cap \mathcal{V}_{c_y} \ne \emptyset \right\}.

So sv(0)=1s_v^{(0)} = 1 exactly when at least one cell of each target cluster appears within distance rr of vv (and vv itself is excluded). The score is symmetric in (cx,cy)(c_x, c_y).

Step 2 — single graph-diffusion step

The raw indicator is sparse. cooccur_local() smooths it once over the kNN graph AA (same construction as in nhood_enrichment()). With D=diag(dv+1)D = \mathrm{diag}(d_v + 1):

sv(1)=sv(0)dv+1+∑uAvusu(0)du+1,i.e.𝐬(1)=(A+I)D−1𝐬(0). \boxed{\; s_v^{(1)} \;=\; \frac{s_v^{(0)}}{d_v + 1} \;+\; \sum_{u} A_{vu} \, \frac{s_u^{(0)}}{d_u + 1}, \quad\text{i.e.}\quad \mathbf{s}^{(1)} \;=\; (A + I)\, D^{-1}\, \mathbf{s}^{(0)}. \;}

Concretely, every cell shares an equal portion of its own indicator with each of its kNN neighbors plus itself. The output column is named cooccur_local_<cluster_x>_<cluster_y>.

With maxnsteps > 1 the step is iterated, each step starting from the previous result: 𝐬(t)=(A+I)D−1𝐬(t−1)\mathbf{s}^{(t)} = (A + I) D^{-1} \mathbf{s}^{(t-1)}. The total ∑vsv\sum_v s_v is conserved. Iteration stops early when the kurtosis of the scores decreases by less than 3 between consecutive steps (checked after step 3). Because 𝐬(0)\mathbf{s}^{(0)} is a 0/1 indicator, its kurtosis usually increases under smoothing, so in practice diffusion stops after 4 steps whenever maxnsteps >= 4. maxnsteps = 0 returns the raw indicator. (Versions <= 0.99.1 recomputed every step from 𝐬(0)\mathbf{s}^{(0)}, so any maxnsteps >= 1 gave the single step above.)

cooccur_local_oe() — calibrated local co-localization

For cell vv with NvN_v other cells within radius rr, of which nA(v)n_A(v) are of type A and nB(v)n_B(v) of type B, the number of A–B pairs is sv=nA(v)nB(v)s_v = n_A(v)\, n_B(v) (nA(nA−1)n_A(n_A - 1) for A = B). Its exact expectation when labels are shuffled over fixed positions is multivariate hypergeometric:

Ev=Nv(Nv−1)KAKBM(M−1), E_v = N_v (N_v - 1)\,\frac{K_A K_B}{M (M - 1)},

with MM the other cells and KA,KBK_A, K_B the A and B cells among them. Both are smoothed with Gaussian weights wvu=exp⁡(−dvu2/2σ2)w_{vu} = \exp(-d_{vu}^2 / 2\sigma^2), σ=h/2\sigma = h/2 (bandwidth =h= h, truncated at hh, self weight 1):

local_log2_oev=log⁡2∑uwvusu+c∑uwvuEu+c. \mathrm{local\_log2\_oe}_v = \log_2 \frac{\sum_u w_{vu} s_u + c}{\sum_u w_{vu} E_u + c}.

The section value is log⁡2(∑vsv/∑vEv)\log_2(\sum_v s_v / \sum_v E_v). Hotspot p-values use BB label shuffles: pv=(1+#{b:s̃v(b)≥s̃v})/(B+1)p_v = (1 + \#\{b : \tilde s^{(b)}_v \ge \tilde s_v\}) / (B + 1) with s̃v=∑uwvusu\tilde s_v = \sum_u w_{vu} s_u, then BH over cells. One neighbour search, O(nk)O(nk); each shuffle is one more pass.

Group comparison — compare_groups()

Per-image scores ypmy_{pm} (image mm of patient pp, e.g. log2_oe) come from nhood_enrichment_per_sample() and related helpers. For every cell-type pair, with the patient as the unit:

  • "wilcox": patient means y‾p=1mp∑mypm\bar y_p = \frac{1}{m_p}\sum_m y_{pm}, Wilcoxon rank-sum (exact for small samples).
  • "lmm": ypm=β0+β1casep+γ⊤cp+up+εpmy_{pm} = \beta_0 + \beta_1\,\mathrm{case}_p + \gamma^\top c_p + u_p + \varepsilon_{pm}, up∼N(0,τ2)u_p \sim N(0, \tau^2), εpm∼N(0,σ2)\varepsilon_{pm} \sim N(0, \sigma^2); test of β1\beta_1 with Satterthwaite degrees of freedom (lmerTest). The group (β0,β1\beta_0, \beta_1) and covariates (γ\gamma) are fixed effects; the patient is a random effect (random intercept upu_p, i.e. value ~ group + covariates + (1 | patient)), so the images of a patient are treated as correlated observations. Patient cannot be a fixed effect: each patient belongs to one group, so patient dummies would be confounded with $eta_1$.
  • "perm": T=y‾¯case−y‾¯controlT = \overline{\bar y}_{\mathrm{case}} - \overline{\bar y}_{\mathrm{control}} compared with patient-level label shuffles (within-patient sign flips for paired data).
  • "signrank": dp=y‾p,post−y‾p,pred_p = \bar y_{p,\mathrm{post}} - \bar y_{p,\mathrm{pre}}, Wilcoxon signed-rank.

Benjamini–Hochberg over pairs. summarize_by_patient() averages images within patient, pair and distance r.

Continuous variables — associate_continuous()

For a patient-level variable xpx_p (CRP, disease activity, age): Spearman correlation of y‾p\bar y_p with xpx_p (default; exact p for small cohorts), linear regression y‾p=β0+β1xp+γ⊤cp+εp\bar y_p = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_p + \gamma^\top c_p + \varepsilon_p, the linear mixed model ypm=β0+β1xp+γ⊤cp+up+εpmy_{pm} = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_p + \gamma^\top c_p + u_p + \varepsilon_{pm} (patient as a random intercept upu_p: value ~ x + covariates + (1 | patient)), or a permutation test that shuffles xpx_p between patients. BH over pairs.

Segmentation-free analysis

Pair correlation of transcripts — pcf_cross(), pcf_matrix()

Transcripts are counted in square bins (YA(u)Y_A(u) = transcripts of gene set A in bin uu, inside the tissue mask WW). With the FFT cross-correlation PAB(h)=∑uYA(u)YB(u+h)P_{AB}(h) = \sum_u Y_A(u)\, Y_B(u + h) and the mask overlap O(h)=∑uW(u)W(u+h)O(h) = \sum_u W(u) W(u + h),

gAB(r)=∑|h|≈rPAB(h)λAλB∑|h|≈rO(h),gABrel(r)=gAB(r)gall(r), g_{AB}(r) = \frac{\sum_{|h| \approx r} P_{AB}(h)}{\lambda_A \lambda_B \sum_{|h| \approx r} O(h)}, \qquad g^{\mathrm{rel}}_{AB}(r) = \frac{g_{AB}(r)}{g_{\mathrm{all}}(r)},

where λ\lambda are mean intensities and gallg_{\mathrm{all}} is the pair correlation of all transcripts. grelg^{\mathrm{rel}} equals observed / expected under gene-label shuffling over fixed transcript positions, the transcript counterpart of log2 O/E; cellularity cancels.

Random-feature log-Gaussian Cox process — fit_spatial_rff()

ybj∼NB(μbj),log⁡μbj=log⁡a+αj+σ0f0(ub)+∑k=1KLjkfk(ub),fk(u)=ϕk(u)⊤γk, y_{bj} \sim \mathrm{NB}(\mu_{bj}),\quad \log \mu_{bj} = \log a + \alpha_j + \sigma_0 f_0(u_b) + \sum_{k=1}^K L_{jk} f_k(u_b), \quad f_k(u) = \phi_k(u)^\top \gamma_k,

with random Fourier features ϕ(u)=2/M[cos⁡(ωm⊤u/ℓ+bm)]m\phi(u) = \sqrt{2/M}\,[\cos(\omega_m^\top u / \ell + b_m)]_m, ωm∼N(0,I)\omega_m \sim N(0, I) (Gundersen, Zhang & Engelhardt, AISTATS 2021). The coordinates ubu_b are observed, so only the fields and loadings are estimated (MAP, L-BFGS-B, analytic gradients). Model pair correlations follow from gAB(r)=exp⁡Cov[log⁡λA(u),log⁡λB(u+r)]g_{AB}(r) = \exp \mathrm{Cov}[\log\lambda_A(u), \log\lambda_B(u + r)]; removing f0f_0 gives the composition version. Because each fkf_k is a function of the coordinates, rff_fields() evaluates the fitted (unit-variance) fields at any point - cell centroids or transcripts - and averages them per cell when a cell id is given.

Residual factors. To look for spatial programs that known structure does not explain, a per-bin, per-gene log offset objo_{bj} is added, log⁡μbj=log⁡a+obj+αj+σ0f0(ub)+∑kLjkfk(ub)\log \mu_{bj} = \log a + o_{bj} + \alpha_j + \sigma_0 f_0(u_b) + \sum_k L_{jk} f_k(u_b). rff_offset() builds objo_{bj} from covariates of the bins (cell-type composition, domains, or an embedding such as PCA, Harmony or SCIGMA) by a ridge-penalised Poisson regression per gene. The penalty λ∑k‖L⋅k‖2\lambda \sum_k \lVert L_{\cdot k} \rVert_2 (ard) shrinks whole factors that are not needed. rff_factor_test() simulates counts from the fitted model without factors, refits, and compares each factor’s strength ‖L⋅k‖2\lVert L_{\cdot k} \rVert_2 with the largest null factor (parametric bootstrap, family-wise over factors).

Gene-level modules — colocalization_gene_matrix(), colocalization_modules(), module_enrichment()

With a disc kernel KrK_r (one FFT convolution per gene),

Pab=∑uYa(u)(Kr*Yb)(u)(−na if a=b),Eab=nanbN(N−1)Pall, P_{ab} = \sum_u Y_a(u)\, (K_r * Y_b)(u) \;(- n_a \text{ if } a = b), \qquad E_{ab} = \frac{n_a n_b}{N (N - 1)}\, P_{\mathrm{all}},

and log⁡2((Pab+c)/(Eab+c))\log_2((P_{ab} + c) / (E_{ab} + c)) is 0 without co-localization. Genes are clustered (average linkage, distance max⁡M−M\max M - M) into modules; module_enrichment() tests any gene sets per module with the hypergeometric test and BH.

search_interaction_spot() — connected-component spots

This function turns a radius-neighborhood graph into discrete “interaction spots” — connected groups of cells that are likely to be acting on each other in a tissue.

Step 1 — radius-neighbor graph

Restrict to a user-provided cell ID list 𝒱⋆⊆𝒱\mathcal{V}^\star \subseteq \mathcal{V}. For each v∈𝒱⋆v \in \mathcal{V}^\star compute Nr(v)N_r(v) via RANN::nn2 (radius search, neighbor cap kk). Build an undirected graph G⋆=(𝒱⋆,E⋆)G^\star = (\mathcal{V}^\star, E^\star) with

E⋆={{v,u}:v∈𝒱⋆,u∈Nr(v)∩𝒱⋆}. E^\star \;=\; \bigl\{\{v, u\} : v \in \mathcal{V}^\star,\; u \in N_r(v) \cap \mathcal{V}^\star\bigr\}.

Step 2 — weak connected components

Run igraph::components(G^\star, mode = "weak"). Each component Γq⊆𝒱⋆\Gamma_q \subseteq \mathcal{V}^\star is a candidate spot, and every cell vv receives an integer label q(v)q(v).

Step 3 — keep target-cluster, size-nminn_\min spots

Define the bounding box of component qq from its cells’ coordinates,

[xqmin,xqmax]×[yqmin,yqmax],nq=|Γq|, \bigl[x_q^{\min}, x_q^{\max}\bigr] \times \bigl[y_q^{\min}, y_q^{\max}\bigr], \quad n_q = |\Gamma_q|,

and keep cell vv in the output iff

c(v)∈𝒯andnq(v)>nmin, c(v) \in \mathcal{T} \quad\text{and}\quad n_{q(v)} > n_\min,

where 𝒯\mathcal{T} is the target_cluster argument. The function returns a tidy data.frame of surviving cells, one row per cell, with columns cluster_id, x_min, x_max, y_min, y_max, and n_all_cells.

Function Unit Local geometry Statistic Test

The multi-sample functions run the single-sample statistics per image and test the per-image values with the patient as the unit; see the case-control tutorial.
